title.zh: 筏羅訶（野豬化身）救起沉没的大地

region.en: Varaha temple, Pushkar (symbolic pin at the ancient Varaha shrine)
region.zh: 布施伽爾野豬神廟（象徵性定位於古筏羅訶聖地）

texts.period: Vishnu Purana, Book I, ch. 4, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840); epic sources older

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, ch. 4 (the Varaha avatar)

summary.en: At the end of the last kalpa, the earth sinks into the waters and the demon Hiranyaksha drags it deeper. Vishnu becomes a boar - the size of an elephant, tusked like a mountain - plunges into the cosmic sea, slays the demon in a battle lasting a thousand years, and raises the earth on his tusk from the abyss, setting it again upon its foundations.
summary.zh: 前一劫之末，大地沉入眾水，惡魔金座（希任耶克沙）將其拖得更深。毘濕奴化身野豬——大如巨象、獠牙如山——躍入宇宙之海，與惡魔搏殺千年，誅之，並以獠牙將大地自深淵托起，重立於其基座之上。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (Varaha temples and iconography across India). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: When the world lay dissolved, the earth, deprived of her place, sank into the waters of the abyss; and the mighty demon Hiranyaksha, seeing her drifting in the deep, seized her and drew her down to his own realm below. The rishis and the gods, helpless, sought the Lord, and praised him, and he heard them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vishnu took the form of a boar, vast as the largest elephant, dark like the tualsi leaf, with tusks white and shining, eyes like the autumn moon; he plunged into the ocean and roared like thunder, and the waters trembled. Hiranyaksha, wrathful, came up from the abyss to meet him, and the two fought - hurling trees, darts, mountains - a battle that the sages measure in a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the boar caught the demon on his tusk and slew him, as Indra slew the foe; then he sought out the earth where she lay in the lower regions, lifted her upon his tusk, glowing like a crescent moon, and rose from the waters. He set the earth upon her own foundations, level and firm as in the beginning, and the seas and rivers returned to their beds; the Brahma-fathers then shaped the world's inhabitants anew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Varaha ('boar') avatar story is the Puranas' principal earth-rescue myth: a cosmogony in which creation is interrupted and restored - the world re-founded by an animal-bodied god.

The setup belongs to the end of time: when the previous kalpa closes, the earth (personified as Bhu-devi) is stripped of her place and sinks into the primordial waters. The demon Hiranyaksha - the golden-eyed Asura whose brother Hiranyakashipu stars in the Narasimha story - finds her drifting in the abyss and drags her down to the demon-realms below, a kidnapping of the planet itself. The gods and seers, unable to cope, praise Vishnu; and Vishnu answers by becoming the most ancient of his forms: a boar.

The transformation is described with relish: vast as the largest elephant, dark, with white shining tusks and eyes like the autumn moon, he roars into the cosmic sea 'like thunder' and dives. The battle with Hiranyaksha is full-scale cosmic combat - trees, darts, mountains hurled; the fight measured by the sages in a thousand years - and the demon's boast (that no god can withstand him) is answered by the boar's tusk. Hiranyaksha is killed, 'as Indra slew the foe', and the boar then descends into the lower regions, finds the earth lying faint on the abyss floor, lifts her upon his tusk - 'glowing like a crescent moon' - and rises from the waters, setting her back upon her foundations 'level and firm as in the beginning'. The rivers and seas return to their beds, and the re-creation of inhabitants proceeds under the Brahma-fathers.

Function: the myth does the work of a second creation story - the world's foundation is not single but cyclical, re-established whenever it sinks; the rescue is agricultural and cosmic at once (the earth as a field lifted from flood-waters is a vividly peasant image; Indra-Vritra's freed rivers are its Vedic cousin). In temple art the scene is rendered monumental - most famously at Mamandur, Eran, and Khajuraho - Vishnu-boar colossal, anthropomorphic, bearing the earth goddess on his arm: one of the largest stone figures in Indian art (the Eran Varaha). Theologically, Varaha is the avatar that shows Vishnu's body as the world's support - the link between the Purusha's cosmic body and the specific rescue of a living landscape. In the cross-tradition matrix, this is the Hindu member of the earth-diver/earth-raiser family (compare the birds of the Yoruba and Woodlands diving for soil, or the Chinese Pangu's corpse becoming the landscape): here the diver is the god himself, and the soil is the goddess.
narrative.zh: 筏羅訶（『野豬』）化身故事是往世書主要的大地救援神話：一部創世被中斷而復原的宇宙志——世界由獸身之神重新奠定。設定屬於時間之末：前一劫閉合之時，大地（人格化為地神 Bhu-devi）被剝離其所居，沉入原初之水。惡魔金座——其弟金輪即是獅面人故事的主角——發現她漂於深淵，將其拖入下方魔域，是對行星本身的綁架。諸神與仙人無力應對，頌讚毘濕奴；毘濕奴以最古老的形態回應：野豬。變身被津津有味地描述：大如巨象、體黑、白獠牙閃亮、目如秋月，他『如雷』般吼入宇宙之海而潛。與金座之戰是全面宇宙戰——擲樹、擲鏢、擲山；仙人以其千年計量——而惡魔的傲語（無神能當其鋒）由野豬之獠牙作答。金座被誅，『如因陀羅誅敵』；野豬繼而下行至下方之境，見大地昏厥於深淵之底，以獠牙托起她——『燦如新月』——自水中升起，將她重置於基座之上，『平坦而堅固，如太初』。諸河諸海歸於河床海床，居民族群的再創造由梵天之父們續行。功能：此神話行使第二創世故事之職——世界的奠基非一次性而是循環的，每逢沉没即被重立；救援既是農事的也是宇宙的（大地如被自洪水中托起的田畝，是鮮明的農人意象；因陀羅釋河是其在吠陀中的表親）。廟宇藝術將此景鑄為巨構——最有名者於馬曼杜、埃蘭與卡朱拉霍——毘濕奴-野豬巨大、擬人、臂承地母：印度藝術中最大的石像之一（埃蘭筏羅訶）。神學上，筏羅訶是顯示毘濕奴之身即世界之基的化身——連接原人的宇宙之身與對活的景觀之特定救援。在跨傳統矩陣中，此為『潛水取土/舉地』家族的印度成員（比較約魯巴與林地傳統中潛水取泥的鳥，或中國盤古屍身化為地貌）：此處潛者即神本身，而泥土即女神。

title.en: The Man-Lion Kills the Unkillable King

region.en: Ahobilam, Andhra Pradesh (principal Narasimha pilgrimage site)
region.zh: 安得拉邦阿霍比拉姆（獅面人首要朝聖地）

texts.period: Vishnu Purana, Book I, chs. 15-19, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, Prahlada and the Narasimha avatar

summary.en: The demon king Hiranyakashipu wins a lawyer's boon - he cannot be killed by man or beast, indoors or out, by day or night, on ground or in air, by any weapon. His son Prahlada worships Vishnu anyway. At dusk, on a threshold, the king challenges a pillar; it splits, and Vishnu steps out as Narasimha - neither man nor beast - and kills him with claws on his lap, neither ground nor sky, at neither day nor night, with no weapon.
summary.zh: 魔王金輪贏得律師式恩諭——人獸皆不能殺之、屋內外皆不能、晝夜皆不能、地上空中皆不能、任何兵器皆不能。其子布羅赫拉達偏偏崇拜毘濕奴。黃昏，於門檻上，王挑釁廊柱；柱裂，毘濕奴化身獅面人那羅辛哈步出——非人非獸——以爪於膝上殺之，非地非天，非晝非夜，不用兵器。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition with major temples (Ahobilam, Simhachalam) and Narasimha Jayanti observances. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Hiranyakashipu, brother of the slain Hiranyaksha, performed savage austerities until Brahma, shaken, granted his boon: let me not be slain by any being created by thee - man or beast, god or demon; let me not die inside a dwelling nor outside it, neither by day nor by night, neither on the ground nor in the air; no weapon shall reach me. Armed with impossibility, he conquered the three worlds and demanded worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 15-16 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: His son Prahlada, from the womb, knew the Lord; taught by sages, taught by Narada, the boy answered every tutor and every torture with the name of Vishnu. His father tried poison, fire, elephants, serpents; the boy was unharmed. Asked where this Vishnu was whom he worshiped, Prahlada said: He is in the pillar, as He is in me; the king, in fury, struck the pillar with his fist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 16-18 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pillar split with a sound like the world cracking, and out stepped a being never before seen: to the waist a man, below a lion, eyes like flame, a mane like midnight. Narasimha - neither man nor beast - seized the demon king at the threshold (neither inside nor out), at dusk (neither day nor night), laid him on his lap (neither ground nor sky), and opened him with his claws (no weapon), at the hour of neither day nor night. The boon survived; the king did not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Prahlada-Narasimha cycle is the Puranas' masterpiece of the boon-and-loophole plot - the tradition's most legally literate myth, in which omnipotence is demonstrated not by raw force but by reading a contract against its grantor.

The boon: Hiranyakashipu, brother of Hiranyaksha (the earth-stealing demon killed by the boar), performs ferocious austerities on the Mandara ridge until Brahma, scorching, grants his carefully drafted immunity: he shall not be slain by any being created by Brahma; not by man or beast, god or demon; not indoors or outdoors; not by day or night; not on ground or in air; not by any weapon; not by anything living or unliving that the creator made. With invulnerability drafted into every clause, he reconquers the three worlds and replaces worship of the gods with worship of himself.

The son: Prahlada - 'delight' - is the wrong kind of child for a demon-king. Instructed in the womb by Narada (the Purana's devotional theology: the name heard before birth takes root), he returns from every schooling with one curriculum: Vishnu is everywhere, in the pillar as in me. The father's countermeasures escalate through the Purana's catalogue of horrors - poison, fire, elephants, serpent-darts - and every attempt fails because the boy's protection is the very god his father excludes. The debates between father and son are the myth's real battleground: theology argued across a throne room.

The pillar: asked by his raging father whether his Vishnu is present in this pillar, Prahlada says yes - and the king strikes the column. It splits 'with a sound like the world cracking', and out steps a being the boon's author never created: Narasimha, to the waist a man, below a lion - outside every drafted category (neither man nor beast; not created by Brahma in any named kind). The kill is staged in the remaining loopholes: at the threshold (neither inside nor outside), at dusk (neither day nor night), on the god's own lap (neither ground nor sky), torn open by claws (no weapon). Each condition of the boon is honored; the king is dead; the contract is fulfilled and destroyed at once.

Aftermath: the gods fear the new form will not calm; Prahlada is asked to pacify him, and the boy's praise (the Prahlada-charita) does so - Narasimha crowns the child king of the demons. The imagery becomes one of the great iconographies of India: Narasimha bursting from the pillar carved on temple walls everywhere, the god's fury and the child's serenity paired.

Function: the story is the charter of bhakti's absolute claim (a child's faith defeats a demon's law) and of Vishnu's preserving justice - the lord answers prayers by arriving precisely where the rules say no one can. It is also the tradition's own satire of magical thinking: the boon that banishes every named possibility is beaten by a possibility the banisher forgot to name. In the boon-curse motif cluster, Narasimha is the perfect case: the boon is honored to the letter and inverted in spirit; the law is kept, and the lawbreaker's world ends.
narrative.zh: 布羅赫拉達-獅面人循環是往世書『恩諭-漏洞』情節的傑作——傳統中最具法律素養的神話：全能不以蠻力示人，而以按合同反治授予者示人。恩諭：金輪——被野豬所誅的竊地魔金座之弟——在曼陀羅山脊行兇暴苦行，直至梵天不堪炙烤而授予其精心起草的不死性：不被梵天所造之任何存在所殺；非人非獸、非神非魔；不在屋內屋外；非晝非夜；不在地上空中；不被任何兵器所及；不被造物主所造之任何有生或無生之物所殺。每一條款皆被豁免之後，他重新征服三界，並以對自身的崇拜取代對諸神的崇拜。其子：布羅赫拉達——意為『喜悅』——是魔王最不想要的兒子。經那羅陀於胎中教授（往世書奉愛神學：出生前聞名，其名生根），他自每一次求學歸來只帶一門課程：毘濕奴無所不在，在柱中亦在我中。父親的對策在往世書的恐怖目錄中升級——毒、火、巨象、蛇鏢——每一計皆敗，因孩童的護佑正是父親所排除的那位神。父子之辯是神話真正的戰場：神學在王座廳中交鋒。廊柱：被狂怒的父親問其毘濕奴是否在此柱中，布羅赫拉達答是——王以拳擊柱。柱『如世界碎裂之聲』裂開，走出一個恩諭作者未曾創造的存在：那羅辛哈，腰以上為人、以下為獅——在每一既定範疇之外（非人非獸；非梵天以任何命名之種所造）。誅殺在剩餘的漏洞中上演：在門檻（非內非外）、在黃昏（非晝非夜）、於神之膝上（非地非天）、以爪撕裂（無兵器）。恩諭的每一條件皆被遵守；王死；合同同時被履行與摧毀。後續：諸神懼新形態不能平息；布羅赫拉達被請去安撫，孩童的讚美（布羅赫拉達頌）奏效——獅面人立孩童為魔王之王。圖像成為印度最偉大的圖像學之一：獅面人自柱中迸出，雕於處處廟牆，神之怒與孩童之靜並列。功能：此故事是奉愛絕對主張的憲章（孩童之信勝魔王之法），也是毘濕奴護持之義——主應祈禱，恰在規則說無人能至之處降臨。它亦是傳統自身的魔法思維諷刺：排除一切已命名可能性的恩諭，被遺忘者未命名的一種可能性擊敗。在恩諭-詛咒母題群中，獅面人是完美案例：恩諭被逐字遵守而在精神上被反轉；法律被遵守，而違法者的世界終結。

functions: Charter of bhakti: a child's devotion defeats a demon's contract with fate
Theology of preserving justice - the god arrives inside the rules' loopholes
Boon-and-loophole plot: the tradition's most legally literate myth
Iconographic charter: the pillar-burst Narasimha in temples across India

title.en: The Dwarf's Three Steps: Vamana and King Bali
title.zh: 侏儒的三步：筏摩那與婆利王

region.en: Thrikkakara, Kerala (Vamana temple of the Onam festival)
region.zh: 喀拉拉邦特里卡卡拉（歐南節之筏摩那神廟）

texts.period: Vishnu Purana, Book I-II (Bali's sacrifice), c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book I, chs. 18-19 and Book II (Bali and the Dwarf avatar)

summary.en: The Asura king Bali, grandson of Prahlada, has conquered the three worlds by sacrifice and virtue, and the gods are homeless. Vishnu is born as a dwarf Brahmin and comes to Bali's great sacrifice asking for three paces of ground. Laughing at the tiny gift, Bali grants it - and the dwarf grows through sky and earth, taking heaven in one stride, earth in the second, and for the third steps on Bali's head, sending him to rule the netherworld. Each year, Bali is allowed home: the Onam festival.
summary.zh: 阿修羅王婆利——布羅赫拉達之孫——以祭祀與德行征服三界，諸神遂無家可歸。毘濕奴化身侏儒婆羅門，來到婆利的大祭上求三步之地。婆利笑許這份微小禮物——侏儒遂長貫天與地，一步取天，二步取地，第三步踏於婆利之首，遣其下治冥界。每年婆利獲准回家：此即歐南節。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Onam is Kerala's principal festival (celebrated across communities, with its own political readings of Bali). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Bali, grandson of the devotee Prahlada, ruled the three worlds by the power of sacrifice; he was just, generous, and invincible. The gods, stripped of their domains, went to Vishnu; and Vishnu, to restore them without breaking the law of the gift, was born as a dwarf Brahmin, Vamana, and came, staff in hand, to the vast sacrifice Bali was performing on the banks of the Narmada.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dwarf asked for a gift: three paces of ground. Bali's preceptor, Shukra, saw the trap and warned him; Bali answered that a Brahmin asking was a gift that could not be measured by size - and made the grant, water poured from his own hand. The dwarf then grew: his head rose through the worlds, the gods assembled in his body; one stride covered heaven, the second the earth and underworlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 18-19 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: For the third step there was nowhere left. Bali bowed his head; Vamana placed his foot upon it and pushed the king down to Patala, the netherworld, of which he was made the lord - honored, not humiliated. Because Bali's virtue was real, Vishnu granted him the annual return: each year, on the day kept as Onam, Bali comes up to see his people, and his kingdom for a day is the world again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Books 1-2 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Vamana-Bali story is the Puranas' most elegant trickster myth - a conquest undone by a gift measured in steps - and it carries the one major Hindu festival whose hero is a demon.

The setup inverts the usual order: Bali, grandson of the great devotee Prahlada, is not a villain but an exemplary king - just, learned, generous, and undefeated because his power is sacrificial merit itself. Under his rule the three worlds are governed well; the problem is bookkeeping: if the Asuras hold everything, the gods have nothing to preside over. The gods complain to Vishnu, who refuses simple conquest - Bali's merit is real and the law of the gift protects it. Vishnu's solution is to be born as a dwarf Brahmin, Vamana ('the dwarf'), and to win back the worlds through the ritual economy: by asking.

The asking is staged at Bali's own great sacrifice on the Narmada's banks. A tiny Brahmin with an umbrella and a water-pot arrives; Bali receives him with full honor and asks his wish. The request - three paces of ground - is comically small, and Bali laughs as he grants it. But Shukra, the Asuras' preceptor, recognizes the shape of the trap (in the fuller tellings, Shukra shrinks himself into the spout of the water-vessel to block the gift, and Vamana blinds him with a blade of grass to clear the spout - the trickster answering the trickster). Bali, knowing the warning and granting anyway, chooses the law of the gift over prudence: a Brahmin's request cannot be refused, and a gift's worth is not its size. The water is poured; the grant is sealed.

Then the growth: Vamana's dwarf body expands through every world - gods assembled in his limbs - and he measures. One stride takes heaven; the second takes earth and the underworlds. For the third, there is nothing left but the giver. Bali bows and offers his own head; Vamana's foot sets upon it, and the king descends to Patala - not as a punished rebel but as the honored lord of the netherworld, a king of sorts still. The worlds return to the gods without a battle and without a broken promise.

The coda is what keeps the story alive: because Bali's virtue was real, Vishnu grants him a yearly return - each year Bali comes up to visit his kingdom and his people. In Kerala this day is Onam: the harvest festival at which households lay flower carpets and a feast (onasadya) to welcome the banished king's homecoming - a demon-king, exiled by the god, celebrated as the best of rulers. The festival's politics are part of the myth's afterlife: in Kerala, Mahabali's golden age is recalled as an era of equality (the proverb: all were equal when Maveli ruled), and modern movements have read Onam as the memory of a just order displaced. The record keeps both readings.

Function: the story teaches the ritual law of the gift (a promise made is a world transferred), the dwarf-as-god theology (smallness that contains all worlds), and the ambivalence of righteous conquest. Comparative readers place it beside the trickster-wager cluster and the three-strides motif known also in Indo-European poetry (the 'three paces' of Vishnu in the Rigveda are already cosmic - the myth is an epic expansion of a Vedic image).
narrative.zh: 筏摩那-婆利故事是往世書最優雅的詭計神話——一場以步為量度的贈禮所瓦解的征服——並且承載著印度教唯一一個以惡魔為主角的重大節日。設定反轉常規：婆利，大信徒布羅赫拉達之孫，並非惡棍而是模範之王——公正、博學、慷慨，因其力量即祭祀功德本身而不可戰勝。其治下三界井然；問題在於記帳：若阿修羅擁有一切，諸神便無所司掌。諸神向毘濕奴陳情，毘濕奴拒絕簡單的征服——婆利的功德真實，贈禮之法護佑之。毘濕奴之解為化身侏儒婆羅門筏摩那（『侏儒』），透過儀式經濟以『求』奪回世界。求取在婆利於納爾默達河畔舉行的大祭上上演。持傘與水罐的小婆羅門到來；婆利以全禮接待，問其所欲。所求——三步之地——小得可笑，婆利笑而允之。但阿修羅國師尸訶認出陷阱的形狀（較全的講述中，尸訶將自己縮入水器壺嘴以阻贈禮，筏摩那以草葉蔽其目以清壺嘴——詭計者對付詭計者）。婆利明知警告而仍允，以贈禮之法取勝於謹慎：婆羅門之求不可拒，禮之價不在其量。水已傾注；許諾封印。隨後是生長：筏摩那的侏儒之身擴張貫穿諸世界——諸神聚於其肢——而後丈量。一步取天；二步取地與冥界。第三步，唯餘施與者。婆利低首獻其頭；筏摩那之足踏其上，王下至缽陀羅（Patala）冥界——非為受罰之叛逆，而為受尊的冥界之主，仍是一種之王。世界未經一戰、未破一諾而歸於諸神。尾聲使故事長存：因婆利之德真實，毘濕奴准其年年歸返——每年婆利上來探望其王國與人民。在喀拉拉，此日即歐南節（Onam）：家家鋪花毯、設盛宴（onasadya）迎接被逐之王的歸來——一位被神放逐的魔王，被尊為最優的統治者。節日的政治是神話後續的一部分：在喀拉拉，摩訶婆利的黃金時代被追憶為平等之世（諺語：瑪韋利在位時人人平等），現代運動亦將歐南讀作被取代的公正秩序之記憶。本錄並存兩種讀法。功能：故事教授贈禮的儀式法（諾成則世界易主）、侏儒即神的神學（含納一切世界之小），以及義戰的曖昧。比較讀者置之於詭計者-賭注母題群與印歐詩歌已知的『三步』意象（梨俱吠陀中毘濕奴的三步已是宇宙性的——此神話是吠陀意象的史詩擴展）。

functions: Ritual law of the gift: a granted promise transfers worlds
Dwarf-theology: smallness containing all worlds (Vedic three strides expanded)
Festival charter of Onam - the annual return of the exiled demon-king
Ambivalence of righteous conquest: merit honored even as it is displaced

title.en: Krishna Born in Prison: The Midnight Child of Mathura
title.zh: 牢中誕生的克里希那：馬圖拉的午夜之子

region.zh: 馬圖拉（克里希那誕生地神廟）

texts.period: Vishnu Purana, Book V, chs. 1-4, c. 300-800 CE (Wilson translation, 1840)

source.work: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, trans. H. H. Wilson (1840), Book V, the birth of Krishna

summary.en: The tyrant Kamsa hears a prophecy - the eighth child of his cousin Devaki will kill him - and imprisons the couple, killing each infant at birth. The eighth child is born at midnight: Vishnu himself, who shows the parents his four-armed form, instructs the father to carry him across the Yamuna to Gokula, and vanishes into the herd-boys' world while a newborn girl is surrendered to Kamsa in his place.
summary.zh: 暴君甘薩聞預言——其表妹德瓦吉之第八子將殺之——遂囚禁夫婦，於每個嬰兒誕生時親手誅之。第八子於午夜誕生：即毘濕奴本人，向父母顯示四臂之形，囑父攜其渡亞穆納河至戈庫拉，隨即隱入牧童世界；甘薩則得一名代死的新生女嬰。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of the highest intensity (Janmashtami, Mathura-Vraja pilgrimage). Classified 'myth' (Puranic narrative rather than scripture's legal sections).

passages.text: A voice from the sky told Kamsa at the wedding of Devaki: the eighth child of this union will slay thee. Kamsa drew his sword at once; Vasudeva pleaded, offering all his children; Kamsa spared the couple but imprisoned them, and destroyed each child as it was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 1-2 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, in the month of Bhadra, the eighth child was born - and the prison filled with light. The parents saw the newborn as Vishnu himself, four-armed, with the conch, discus, mace and lotus; the babe spoke: take me to Nanda's house in Gokula and put the girl-child just born there in my place. Vasudeva carried him through the barred doors, the guards slept, the Yamuna parted, and the exchange was made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 3-4 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kamsa came for the child, seizing the girl to dash her against stone; she slipped from his hands into the sky as the goddess, prophesying: thy destroyer lives, thy death is certain. Kamsa thereupon ordered the massacre of all infants in his realm; but the child grew up in Gokula among herdsmen as Krishna, son of Nanda and Yashoda - known in the village only as a darling, dark, and fond of butter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 5, chs. 4-6 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana, London, 1840 (public domain); modern sourcebook: Edwin F. Bryant, Krishna: A Sourcebook, Oxford, 2007

narrative.en:
The birth of Krishna in the Vishnu Purana is the tradition's fullest miracle-birth narrative - the infant god born under a death sentence, smuggled across a river, and raised in disguise as a cowherd's child.

The prophecy: at the wedding of his cousin Devaki to Vasudeva, a voice from the sky stops Kamsa's chariot: the eighth child of this marriage will kill you. Kamsa's response is immediate tyrant-logic: he seizes the couple, and - persuaded by Vasudeva to spare them - confines them in a guarded chamber and destroys each child at birth, one by one. The Purana is unsparing: six children die at their father-uncle's hands.

The eighth child: on the eighth day of the dark fortnight (the night kept today as Janmashtami), in the rain-month Bhadra, Devaki bears the eighth child at midnight - and the dungeon fills with light. The newborn is Vishnu himself: the parents see him four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus - and the babe speaks, instructing them in the escape he has arranged. The theology is exact: this is not a god's avatara arriving later, but the lord born knowingly, giving orders as an infant.

The escape: Vasudeva carries the child out through the locked doors - the guards sunk in sleep by divine power, the chains unfastened, the Yamuna river (in flood, in the later tellings) parting or subsiding as he crosses to the herdsman's village of Gokula. There he exchanges the infant for the girl-child just born to Yashoda, Nanda's wife, and returns to his cell with the substitute. When Kamsa comes to kill the eighth child, the girl slips from his grip, rises into the air as the goddess, and prophesies his death - the tyrant is left with a massacre decree and no victim.

The disguise: the child grows in Gokula and Vraja as Krishna - 'the dark one' - darling of the cowherds, stealing butter, laughing, suckled by Yashoda who has no idea whose son she is raising. The Purana lets the disguise run for years before the prophecy closes: Kamsa's massacre (the slaughter of infants in his realm - a detail the Christian birth narrative mirrors, as scholars from Weber onward have noted), the demon attempts (Putana the poison-nurse among them in later books), and at last the wrestling-arena confrontation where the grown Krishna kills the tyrant who ordered his death at birth.

Function: this is the master narrative of Janmashtami, kept by fast and midnight vigil across India - the devotees imitate the vigil of the prison night. Theologically it fuses the avatara doctrine with the bhakti child-god: the same lord who is the cosmic sleeper on the waters is a baby that must be smuggled and hidden - omnipotence choosing helplessness, the adult god's disguise as a vulnerable child being the religion's central emotional engine. The birth scene's comparisons are direct: across the biblical mass-slaughter birth (Ramayana's and Christian telling both), the child smuggled past a tyrant is one of the world's oldest rescue plots; the Purana's version is distinctive in making the child the author of his own escape.
narrative.zh: 毘濕奴往世書中克里希那的誕生是該傳統最完整的奇蹟誕生敘事——嬰神在死刑之下誕生、被偷渡過河、偽裝為牧童之子養大。預言：表妹德瓦吉與婆藪提婆成婚之時，天外之聲止住甘薩的車：此婚之第八子將殺你。甘薩的反應是即刻的暴君邏輯：他抓住夫婦，經婆藪提婆求情饒其性命，將其囚於守衛之室，並在每個孩子誕生時逐一誅之。往世書毫不留情：六個孩子死於這位伯父之手。第八子：於黑半月初八之夜（今日守為建摩斯陀密節之夜）、雨月巴陀羅月，德瓦吉於午夜誕下第八子——牢獄充滿光芒。新生兒即毘濕奴本人：父母見其四臂，持法螺、輪、杵、蓮——而嬰兒開口，指示他已安排好的逃亡。神學精確：非神的化身後至，而是主自知而生，以嬰兒之身下達命令。逃亡：婆藪提婆抱子穿過緊鎖之門——守衛因神力沉睡，鎖鏈自解，泛濫的亞穆納河（後世講述中）在他渡往牧村戈庫拉時分開或退落。在那裡他以嬰兒換取耶雪陀（南陀之妻）剛生的女嬰，攜替身回獄。甘薩前來誅殺第八子時，女嬰自其掌中滑出，升空化為女神，預言其死——暴君落得一道屠殺令而無受害者。偽裝：孩子以克里希那——『黑者』——之名在戈庫拉與牧區長大，牛倌的寵兒，偷酪、嬉笑，由耶雪陀哺乳，而她並不知自己養的是誰的兒子。往世書讓偽裝持續多年，直至預言閉合：甘薩的屠殺（境內嬰兒盡誅——學者自韋伯以降皆注意到此細節與基督教誕生敘事的呼應）、妖魔的試探（後卷中的毒乳女普塔那等），最終在摔角場上，長成的克里希那誅殺那位在其誕生時即下令殺他的暴君。功能：此為建摩斯陀密節（Janmashtami）的主敘事，全印以齋戒與午夜守夜守持——信徒模仿牢獄之夜的守候。神學上它熔化身 doctrine 與奉愛的兒童神：臥於水上宇宙之眠的同一主，也是必須被偷渡與藏匿的嬰孩——全能選擇無助，成年神偽裝為易受傷的孩童，是此宗教情感的核心引擎。誕生場景的比較是直接的：跨越聖經的屠嬰誕生（羅摩衍那與基督教講述皆有），被偷渡越過暴君的孩子是世界上最古老的救援情節之一；往世書版本的獨特處在於讓孩子成為自己逃亡的作者。

functions: Master narrative of Janmashtami (midnight fast and vigil across India)
Avatara doctrine fused with the bhakti child-god: omnipotence choosing helplessness
Rescue plot of the doomed child smuggled past a tyrant
Pilgrimage charter of Mathura-Vraja (Janmabhoomi and Gokula sites)

title.en: Jimutavahana Gives His Body to the Garudas
title.zh: 吉穆多伐訶那以身餵金翅鳥

region.en: Malaya mountain, Vidyadhara realm (symbolic pin in the Vindhya uplands)
region.zh: 摩羅耶山，飛天國境（象徵性定位於溫迪亞高地）

texts.period: Kathasaritsagara of Somadeva, c. 1070 CE, Kathapitha-lambaka, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney translation, 1880)

source.work: The Katha Sarit Sagara; or, Ocean of the Streams of Story, trans. C. H. Tawney (1880), vol. 1, the story of Jimutavahana

summary.en: Jimutavahana, prince of the Vidyadharas, renounces his throne for the life of a wandering ascetic and comes to a mountain where Garudas yearly carry off a Naga to eat. Finding a weeping serpent-child bound for the feast, he takes his place in the stone trough, offers his own body, and endures the voracious bird's first bite - whereupon the Garuda stops, transformed: the age of eating Nagas ends, and the prince, restored, is married to the princess he rescued on the way.
summary.zh: 飛天國王子吉穆多伐訶那放棄王位，過雲遊苦行生活，來到一座金翅鳥每年攫食一蛇的山。見一為盛宴被縛而泣的蛇童，他代之臥於石槽，獻出自己的身體，忍受貪饞之鳥的第一啄——金翅鳥遂止，轉化：食蛇之世終結；王子復原，娶途中相救的公主。

sensitivity.note: Secular-legendary katha literature read within living Sanskrit-katha traditions; the story also exists as the Buddhist-inflected Nagananda play tradition. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Jimutavahana, eldest of the Vidyadhara princes, felt no joy in a throne: he gave the kingdom to his brother and set out to wander, having freed the prisoners of his father's realm and taken nothing. On his way he restored to life the son of a merchant slain by a snake, and won the love of Malayavati; then, still seeking nothing, he came with his retinue to the slopes of Malaya mountain, where he heard weeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: The weeper was a young Naga, bound and laid in a stone trough: once in every while, he said, the Garudas carry off one of our race and eat him, and this day the lot is mine. Jimutavahana, holding compassion dearer than his own body, bound the child, carried him home to his family, and laid himself in the trough in his place, oiling his own body to make it a proper meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Garuda came, great as the clouds at the world's end, and fixed his beak in the prince's shoulder; the flesh gave way, and Jimutavahana, bleeding, did not move or cry out - only prayed that his sacrifice be accepted. The bird, tasting him, stopped: this flesh is not a serpent's, he said, and learned from the dying prince who he was. The Garuda wept, restored the body with heavenly charms, and vowed before fire that no Naga should ever be seized again; the age of eating serpents ended that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Nagas, led by the rescued child's father, arrived to honor the sacrifice and found their intended victim alive; the prince was healed, married Malayavati, and returned to rule - a king whose throne had been refused and whose body had been spent, and who thereby ended a whole species' predator-prey war with one act of lying still.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kathasaritsagara, tarangas 22-24 (Tawney 1880); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. H. Tawney, The Katha Sarit Sagara; or, Ocean of the Streams of Story, Calcutta, 1880-84 (public domain); annotated: N. M. Penzer, The Ocean of Story, 10 vols., 1924-28

narrative.en:
Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story', c. 1070) is Sanskrit literature's great story-collection - a Kashmiri recasting of the Brihatkatha cycle - and among its most celebrated episodes is the self-sacrifice of Jimutavahana, a story so beloved that the playwright Harsha made it the plot of the Nagananda, and Buddhist storytellers adopted it as a Jataka-style exemplar.

The prince who refuses: Jimutavahana ('whose chariot is the clouds'), eldest son of a Vidyadhara king, is the anti-hero of inheritance: he frees all prisoners in his father's realm, hands the throne to his brother, and walks out to be a wandering ascetic 'taking nothing'. On the road the story layers its ethics: he restores to life a merchant's son dead of snakebite (compassion already outranking death), and wins - almost involuntarily - the love of the princess Malayavati, whose father offers her; the prince, pledged to renunciation, is gently maneuvered by the narrative into accepting a marriage he did not seek.

The mountain: arriving at Malaya with his retinue, he hears weeping and follows it. A young Naga - serpent-being of the underworld race - is bound in a stone trough: by covenant of long standing, the Garudas (the great golden raptor-birds, enemies of the Nagas) periodically seize one of the serpent race and eat him; this day the lot has fallen to this child. Jimutavahana's decision is made without drama: he binds the child, carries him home to his parents, and lies down in the trough himself, anointing his own body with oil 'to make it a proper meal' - the story's black-comic realism in one gesture.

The feeding: the Garuda descends, 'great as the clouds at the world's end', and drives its beak into the prince's shoulder. Flesh tears; the prince does not cry out, does not move - he prays only that his gift be accepted. The bird, mid-bite, stops: this flesh is not a serpent's. From the dying man it learns who he is, and the predator's transformation is the story's climax: the Garuda weeps, restores the torn body with celestial charms (the resurrection beat), and vows before fire that no Naga shall ever again be seized. The Nagas arrive with garlands to mourn their savior and find him alive; the covenant of predation ends in a single act of stillness.

Function: the tale is the katha literature's ethics of ahimsa dramatized - the prince's self-gift does what no battle could, ending a war between species by feeding it. It is the Hindu-courts' answer to the Buddhist Jataka of the Bodhisattva feeding himself to a tigress (the mother-tigress story): shared grammar of compassionate self-donation, resurrection, and conversion of the predator. In Penzer's annotated Ocean of Story the episode's afterlives are traced: Harsha's Nagananda play (7th c.) built a full drama on it, stage traditions in Kerala (Nagananda-based performance) and modern retellings keep it current. Within the motif clusters, the story pairs with resurrection and parable-teaching: the body given is restored, and the restored body becomes a teaching that reforms an entire race of eaters.
narrative.zh: 索摩提婆的《故事海》（kathasaritsagara，約 1070 年）是梵語文學偉大的故事集——對《大故事》循環的克什米爾重鑄——其中最受讚頌的情節之一即吉穆多伐訶那的捨身，故事如此受愛戴，以致戲劇家曷沙王以其情節作《龍喜記》（Nagananda），佛教說書人亦採之為 Jataka 式典範。拒絕王位的王子：吉穆多伐訶那（『雲為其車』），飛天國王之長子，是繼承權的反英雄：他釋放父國的所有囚犯，將王位讓與其弟，徒步出走為雲遊苦行者『一無所取』。途中故事層疊其倫理：他復活一位死於蛇咬的商人之子（慈悲已勝過死亡），並幾乎不自願地贏得公主摩羅耶伐蒂之愛；誓願出離的王子被敘事溫和地推入一場他未曾求取的婚姻。山：攜隨從至摩羅耶山，聞泣聲而循之。一位年幼的龍族（Naga）——地下蛇族——被縛於石槽：依古老盟約，金翅鳥（Garuda，蛇族之大敵）定期攫取蛇族一人食之；此日籤落此童。吉穆多伐訶那的決定毫無戲劇性：他縛起孩童，送回其父母家中，自己臥入石槽，以油塗身『使其為一頓像樣的餐食』——故事黑色喜劇式的寫實盡在一舉。餵食：金翅鳥降臨，『大如世界之末的雲』，喙入王子之肩。血肉撕裂；王子不出聲、不動——只祈他的贈禮被接受。鳥於啄食中停頓：此肉非蛇肉。自垂死者處得知其為誰，捕食者的轉化即故事的高潮：金翅鳥泣，以天界咒法復其撕裂之軀（復活節拍），並於火前立誓：蛇族永不再被攫。龍族攜花環而來哀悼其救主，卻見其生還；捕食的盟約在一次次靜止的行動中終結。功能：此篇是 katha 文學中不害（ahimsa）倫理的戲劇化——王子的捨身做了任何戰爭都做不到的事，以餵食結束兩族的戰爭。它是梵廷宮廷文學對佛教本生經中菩薩捨身餵虎母故事的回應：共享的語法是慈悲捨身、復活、捕食者的皈依。彭澤爾註釋版《故事之洋》追溯了此篇的後續：曷沙的《龍喜記》（七世紀）據此構築全劇，喀拉拉的舞台傳統（基於《龍喜記》的演出）與現代重述使其至今流傳。在母題群中，此篇與復活及譬喻說法相配：被給出的身體被復原，而復原的身體成為改革整個食者之族的教導。

functions: Ethics of ahimsa dramatized: self-gift ends a war between species
Resurrection motif in katha literature - the torn body restored and the predator converted
Hindu-court counterpart of the Buddhist self-donation Jatakas
Charter of Harsha's Nagananda play and Kerala performance tradition

variants.name: Nagananda of King Harsha (7th c. CE)
variants.summary: The story staged as a five-act play with the Bodhisattva-flavored Jimutavahana and the goddess Gauri's intervention; the play's popularity fixed the tale in court and temple performance.

variants.name: Buddhist Jataka parallels (the tigress and the hare)
variants.summary: The Bodhisattva's self-feeding to a starving animal: shared grammar of compassionate self-donation and the predator's transformation; the katha version is its Sanskrit-court cousin.

variants.name: Garuda-Naga covenant endings elsewhere
variants.summary: In most Purana tellings the Garuda-Naga enmity ends by contract (elbow-shells of amrita, the wager of the stakes); the katha version ends it by sacrifice instead - law versus love.
